extracted.intended_audience: academic authors and researchers preparing responses to peer reviewer comments (manuscript submitters)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for drafting diplomatic, evidence-based rebuttals and point-by-point responses to peer reviewer comments during manuscript revision. Focuses on when to push back, how to justify disagreement, escalation to editors, and formatting the response.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to disagree
rubrics_metrics.description: Disagree when the comment would fundamentally compromise your paper's contribution; disagree when it contains a clear factual error; disagree when it asks for something impossible given your resources or timeline. Don't disagree over style preferences or minor methodological suggestions that don't affect your conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never disagree without providing specific evidence for your position. Never disagree on more than 20% of a reviewer's comments, because then you look defensive and difficult. The green lights: factual corrections with citations, scope clarifications where the reviewer misunderstood your question, resource constraints for infeasible experiments. Everything else is gray territory where judgment determines whether to compromise, partially address, or respectfully explain limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenge reviewer statements that are objectively wrong and can be documented with citations or data (e.g., incorrect claims about prior literature or established facts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific sources, quote exact figures, and reference established methods to correct the record. Example: cite multiple peer-reviewed studies that contradict the reviewer's factual claim and revise the manuscript to reflect those citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope misunderstandings
rubrics_metrics.description: Disagree when a reviewer is asking you to answer a different research question than the one your paper addresses (e.g., they want chronic outcomes when you study acute responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the research question, explain why the suggested work lies outside scope, and show what evidence in the paper already addresses the core concern. Revise the manuscript to make scope explicit where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion overreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not acquiesce when a reviewer is expressing personal methodological preference as if it were a requirement (e.g., insisting on one assay when multiple valid approaches exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show objective evidence that the method you used is valid (citations, prior uses) and, if appropriate, offer limited concessions (additional explanation, discussion of alternatives) rather than capitulation to preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and evidence: acknowledge then present evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with acknowledgment of the reviewer's concern, then present the factual evidence and specific manuscript changes that support your disagreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arguing from authority (e.g., 'As experts we believe...'); instead argue from evidence: cite specific sources, quote figures, reference methods. Offer compromises when possible (e.g., discuss limitations and suggest future work). Example phrasing is provided in the article showing acknowledgement, citation of multiple studies, and a statement of manuscript revision (page/lines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to impossible requests (resource/ethical/timeline constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reviewer requests experiments or data collection that are infeasible, document the specific constraints (cost, equipment access, IRB/ethical limits, or time/funding limitations) clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete figures where possible (e.g., instrument costs, time estimates, IRB protocol numbers), explain why the request cannot be completed within the revision window, and always offer alternatives (e.g., new discussion text, acknowledging as limitation, proposing future work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation: when to involve the editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring the editor into the conversation when reviewer behavior is improper or when disagreements affect the core claim and cannot be resolved diplomatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Escalation triggers include reviewers demanding citation of their own work without justification, making personal attacks, or requesting duplication of their unpublished work. Address escalation separately to the editor, quote the problematic reviewer text, present specific examples and evidence, and explain how this violates peer review norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common failure patterns to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Behaviors that turn a defensible disagreement into a career- or paper-harming response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: arguing the reviewer is wrong without showing manuscript clarifications; using disagreement to avoid narrowing an overstated claim; escalating tone instead of fixing issues; emotional phrasing ('unfair'), expertise boasts ('we are leaders with 50 publications'), the 'kitchen sink' approach of disputing most comments, and 'non-response responses' that merely state disagreement without reasoning. Each is accompanied by explanation of why editors dislike it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision framework: disagree / compromise / accept
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple test for handling each reviewer comment: disagree when it contains documentable factual errors, compromises core findings, or demands impossible work; compromise when the reviewer has a point but overreaches; accept when the change strengthens the paper without altering conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick test suggested: If accepting makes the paper better science, accept. If accepting makes it different science, consider disagreeing. If accepting makes the paper impossible to complete, definitely disagree. Emphasize proportionality and leaving the editor with a stronger paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on scope of disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not disagree with more than ~20% of a reviewer's comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disagreeing on a large fraction of comments makes authors look defensive and difficult; editors notice patterns and may be less sympathetic. Pick battles carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and formatting of the response
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a point-by-point response that restates the reviewer concern and pairs each response with the exact evidence or revision (e.g., manuscript page and line numbers). Turn the response into a visible checklist or matrix before finalizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors appreciate clarity and traceability: restate concern in neutral language, provide a concise answer, show where the manuscript was changed (or explain why not), and use tables or matrices to make the changes obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist for respectful disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: A pre-send checklist to ensure disagreements are professional and useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items: restate the reviewer concern in neutral language; identify the valid scientific issue hidden in the comment; point to the exact manuscript change, analysis, or limitation statement that answers it; narrow the claim if evidence is weaker; remove emotional/adversarial phrasing; ask whether an editor could read the exchange and conclude you acted in good faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: What editors care about
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors evaluate the response exchange for professionalism, evidence-based reasoning, constructive dialogue, and whether the authors repaired or improved the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors are looking for discipline in responses rather than whether the reviewer was perfectly fair. A well-crafted disagreement that leaves the manuscript stronger can increase acceptance chances. Avoid language that suggests personal grievance or defensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer alternatives when refusing a request
rubrics_metrics.description: When you cannot perform the requested work, propose credible alternatives that address the reviewer's underlying concern (e.g., additional analysis, clarifying text, noting limitation and future work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always accompany a refusal with a path forward: discuss how future research could address the gap, add discussion of limitations, or perform a bounded analysis that is feasible within constraints.
